questions.q: Why does the held-out grid use a seed never used during training?
options: To make the evaluation run faster
To ensure the (date_range_days, territory) combinations being evaluated were never seen during training
Because stable-baselines3 requires a different seed for evaluation
To reduce the number of held-out episodes needed
questions.explain: Evaluating on episodes the policy never trained on is what makes the held-out comparison meaningful evidence rather than a check on memorized cases.

questions.q: What is being compared on each held-out episode?
options: Two different agents trained with different random seeds
The agent's chosen-hint logical reads vs. the optimizer's own default-plan (action 0) logical reads, on the same sampled parameters
The agent's logical reads on this episode vs. its logical reads on the previous episode
The training-time reward vs. the evaluation-time reward
questions.explain: The comparison holds the sampled date range and territory fixed and measures the agent's chosen hint against the optimizer's own no-hint default plan on that same episode.

questions.q: What was this project's reported win-or-tie rate against the optimizer's default plan on the held-out grid?
options: 34% of episodes
50% of episodes
78% of episodes
100% of episodes
questions.explain: The agent matched or beat the optimizer's own default plan on 78% (187 of 240) of held-out episodes.

questions.q: Where does the boundary-case regression failure mode occur?
options: On every episode regardless of date range
Only on territories with the largest customer counts
On date ranges roughly between 10 and 18 days, near the narrow/wide transition
Only when the agent picks action 0
questions.explain: The agent's losses cluster around the narrow/wide transition zone, where it sometimes still picks FORCE ORDER and loses to the optimizer's default plan.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that comparing against the optimizer's own default plan, rather than a synthetic worst-case benchmark, is the honest evaluation choice?
options: Because synthetic benchmarks are harder to compute than real queries
Because SQL Server's optimizer is already a competent, cost-based baseline, so beating it is a genuinely meaningful result rather than beating a strawman
Because action 0 is the only valid action in evaluation
Because a synthetic benchmark would require a second database
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes that the optimizer's own plan is a strong baseline, so a win-or-tie rate measured against it is more meaningful than one measured against an artificially weak comparison.
